chunks: From him, from Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from Safwan, from Dawud ibn al-Husayn, from 'Umar ibn Hanzalah, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about two men from our companions who had a dispute between them regarding a debt or inheritance, and they submitted themselves for judgment to the Sultan and the judges; is that permissible?

He (peace be upon him) said: "Whoever submits to them in a right or wrong matter, has only submitted to Taghut (divine sovereigns); and whatever is judged for him is only illicit gain (suh't), even if his right is established, because he took it by the judgment of Taghut, and Allah (Exalted is He) commanded that it be disbelieved in."
Allah (Exalted is He) said: 'They submit to Taghut, although they were commanded to disbelieve in it.'

He said: "And how should they act?" He said: "They should look among you to whoever has narrated our hadith, examined our halal and haram, and known our rulings; let them accept him as an arbitrator, for I have made him an arbitrator over you."

So when he judges with our judgment, and they do not accept it from him, then they have slighted the judgment of Allah and referred it to us; and whoever refers to us has referred to Allah, and he is on the verge of shirk (polytheism) with Allah."

I said: "Indeed, each of them chose a man, and both differed in our hadith." He said: "The judgment is what the more just, more knowledgeable, more truthful in the hadith, and more pious of the two judges." And do not pay attention to what the other one judges."

He said: Then I said: "Indeed, both are just and acceptable among our companions, neither excelling the other." He said: "Look at their narration regarding that which your companions have agreed upon; take that from our judgment and leave the unique (shadh) one that is not well-known among your companions."

For that upon which there is agreement, there is no doubt in it. And indeed, matters are three: a matter whose guidance is clear, so it is followed; a matter whose error is clear, so it is avoided; and a difficult matter whose judgment is referred to Allah (Exalted and Mighty).

And the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'Halal is clear and Haram is clear, and between that are doubts (shubuhat); whoever leaves the doubts, he is saved from the prohibited things, and whoever takes the doubts, he commits the prohibited things and perishes from where he does not know.'

I said: "If the two reports from you are well-known, and the trustworthy have narrated them from you." He said: "Look at that whose judgment agrees with the judgment of the Book and the Sunnah and differs from the general public; take it and leave that whose judgment differs from the judgment of the Book and the Sunnah and agrees with the general public."

I said: "May I be your ransom, tell me if the two jurists were ignorant of knowing its ruling from the Book and Sunnah, and we found one of the two reports agreeing with the general public and the other differing from them; which of the two reports should we take?"

He said: "With that which differs from the general public, for indeed in it is guidance." I said: "May I be your ransom, if both reports agree with them." He said: "Look to what their judges and jurists incline towards; leave that and take the other."

I said: "If their judges agreed with both reports." He said: "If that is the case, then defer it until you meet your Imam, for standing firm at the doubts is better than plunging into the perditions."

key_terms.إِمَامَكَ: Imamaka (your Imam, referring to the infallible Imam)
key_terms.الشُّبُهَات: Shubuhat (doubts or ambiguous matters between clear halal and haram)
key_terms.الطَّاغُوت: Taghut (divine sovereigns/authority, often referring to secular rulers)
key_terms.الْمُجْمَعَ عَلَيْهِ: Al-mujma'a 'alayh (that upon which there is consensus/agreement)

ai.seo_question: How do Shia Muslims resolve legal disputes and select the correct religious ruling when there are conflicting narrations?
ai.summary: This foundational hadith from Al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib* establishes the doctrine of *al-Hukm al-Shar'i* (the jurist's ruling), asserting that submission to secular courts constitutes submission to *Taghut* (idols/tyrants). It provides a rigorous epistemological framework for resolving conflicting narrations (*ikhtilaf al-akhbar*) by prioritizing rulings that oppose the general public (*khilaf al-'amma*) and deferring to the Imam in cases of persistent doubt (*tawqif*), thereby laying the groundwork for the later development of the Marja'iyyah system.
